questions.problem: Find the points of intersection of the parabola ${y}^{2}=3(x-2)$ with the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
When the parabola intersects the $y$-axis, we must have $x=0.$ So, we set $x=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =3(0-2) \\ {y}^{2} & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, as the equation ${y}^{2}=-6$ has no solutions, we conclude that there are no intersection points.

questions.problem: Find the points of intersection of the parabola ${x}^{2}=\frac{3}{7}(y+4)$ with the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =\frac{3}{7}(0+4) \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{12}{7} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{12}{7}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the intersection points are
 $(\sqrt{\frac{12}{7}},0)$ and $(-\sqrt{\frac{12}{7}},0).$

questions.problem: Find the point of intersection of the parabola ${y}^{2}-x+10y+21=0$ with the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-x+10y+21 & =0 \\ (0)^{2}-x+10(0)+21 & =0 \\ -x+21 & =0 \\ x & =21\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parabola intersects the $x$-axis at $(21,0).$

questions.problem: Find the point of intersection of the parabola ${y}^{2}+18x-27y+54=0$ with the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0)^{2}+18x-27(0)+54 & =0 \\ 18x+54 & =0 \\ 18x & =-54 \\ x & =-\frac{54}{18} \\ x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parabola intersects the $x$-axis at $(-3,0).$

What is the $x$-intercept of the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has a vertex at $(9,4)$ and passes through the point $(-7,12).$

The general standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h).
$$

Substituting $(h,k)=(9,4)$ into the above gives

$$
(y-4)^{2}=4p(x-9).
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(-7,12),$ we substitute $x=-7$ and $y=12$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(12-4)^{2} & =4p(-7-9) \\ 64 & =4p\cdot (-16) \\ p & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-4)^{2} & =-4(x-9).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0-4)^{2} & =-4(x-9) \\ 16 & =-4(x-9) \\ -4 & =x-9 \\ x & =-4+9 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercept is $5.$

The general standard equation of an up- or down-opening parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k).
$$

Substituting $(h,k)=(-3,4)$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =4p(y-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(0,-5),$ we substitute $x=0$ and $y=-5$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(0+3)^{2} & =4p(-5-4) \\ 9 & =4p(-9) \\ p & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =-(y-4).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =-(0-4) \\ (x+3)^{2} & =4 \\ x+3 & =\pm \sqrt{4} \\ x & =\pm 2-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, from left to right, the $x$-intercepts are $-5$  and $-1.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the points of intersection of the parabola $(y-2)^2=4(x+1)$ with the $y$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the points of intersection of the parabola with the $y$-axis, we set $x=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-2)^{2} & =4(x+1) \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4(0+1) \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4 \\ y-2 & =\pm 2 \\ y & =2\pm 2 \\ y & =0,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parabola intersects the $y$-axis $(0,0)$ and $(0,4).$
